Choose by whether you need many rotating IPs or a few stable ones.

blocks.text: Proxys.io in 2026: what you get

Proxys.io is a per-IP proxy shop rather than a bandwidth network. Its catalog covers shared IPv4 (up to three users per IP), dedicated IPv4, cheap IPv6 from $0.13 per address, premium residential IPv4, rotating residential packages and SIM-based mobile proxies. You rent each IP for days or months, bandwidth is generally unlimited on dedicated IPs, and a 24-hour refund window replaces a trial. It is popular with affiliate marketers and multi-account operators who want fixed addresses rather than a rotating pool.

Strengths: Low-entry per-address products; a provider-reported 100M+ residential network; country, region and city targeting; HTTP/HTTPS/SOCKS5 included; a 24-hour refund window. Weak spots: Rotating mobile traffic pricing must be checked in the cart; residential plans have 30/60/90-day validity; published pool totals do not guarantee reachable IPs; independent target-specific performance has not been established here.
Rayobyte in 2026: what you get

Rayobyte is a US proxy company that started life as Blazing SEO and built its name on dedicated datacenter proxies. Residential proxies have since become its main product. It sells them pay-as-you-go in four volume bands with traffic that never expires, sources at least part of its residential pool in-house, and offers country, region and city targeting. The notable limit is protocol support: its residential gateway does not support SOCKS5 or UDP.

Strengths: Non-expiring residential traffic; Steep volume discounts down to $0.90/GB; Excellent datacenter and ISP catalog; Well-regarded human support. Weak spots: No SOCKS5 or UDP on residential; Pool size not prominently published; Fewer advanced targeting options than enterprise providers.
Pricing: Proxys.io vs Rayobyte

PROXYS.IO separates traffic-based plans from per-address rentals. Rotating residential starts at $1.50/GB on 30, 60 or 90-day plans, without an IP or session cap. Static monthly starting prices are IPv6 $0.13, dynamic $0.27, shared IPv4 $0.67 (up to three users), foreign individual IPv4 $1.47, Windows-fingerprint IPv4 $1.87 and premium static residential IPv4 $3.60. Dedicated mobile IPv4 with unlimited traffic on a private channel starts at $56.79/month. Rotating mobile traffic is priced by the cart slider; no single starting per-GB rate has been confirmed. HEAT_RES provides 35% off eligible residential pay-per-traffic plans. Minimum static rental is one month and the refund window is 24 hours.
Rayobyte prices residential traffic in four pay-as-you-go bands: $3.50/GB for 1-49 GB, $2/GB for 50-249 GB, $1.50/GB for 250-999 GB and $0.90/GB for 1-5 TB. Traffic does not expire.

At 10 GB, a like-for-like total is harder to state because Proxys.io does not publish an exact price for that volume; Rayobyte comes to about $35. At 100 GB, a like-for-like total is harder to state because Proxys.io does not publish an exact price for that volume; Rayobyte comes to about $200. Look past the per-GB figure too. Rayobyte lets unused traffic carry forward, while Proxys.io's allowance does not (30/60/90-day traffic validity; minimum one-month static rental). For irregular workloads, that difference can outweigh a small gap in list price.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

Proxys.io and Rayobyte do not publish a clear residential pool figure, so a size comparison is not possible on published data. Proxys.io reports 100M+ addresses and Rayobyte lists 'Not prominently published'. In practice, what matters is how many unique IPs you get in the countries you target, which you can measure in a short trial by sending a few thousand requests and counting distinct exit addresses. For coverage, Proxys.io lists 195 residential countries, with separate mobile and static coverage countries and Rayobyte lists Global. On targeting, Proxys.io offers country, region and city for residential traffic, with city/carrier selection for mobile, while Rayobyte offers country, region and city.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Protocol support is a real difference here. Proxys.io supports HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS5, while Rayobyte offers HTTP, HTTPS (no SOCKS5 on residential). If your tooling needs SOCKS5, for example some anti-detect browsers, desktop apps or non-HTTP traffic, that settles it in Proxys.io's favour. On sessions, Proxys.io offers static per-IP proxies; rotating residential and mobile, and Rayobyte offers rotates per request by default; sticky sessions available. Setup works the same way on both: a single gateway endpoint, with location and session options passed as username parameters, plus IP whitelisting if you prefer not to use credentials.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: compare the exact target and traffic plan before choosing. PROXYS.IO reports a 100M+ rotating residential network across 195 countries, in addition to static rentals. Pool size alone does not establish success rate; this brief does not independently benchmark PROXYS.IO against the other provider.

SERP and rank tracking: close call. Both are reasonable choices here. Proxys.io: cheap IPv6 can handle some search tasks. Rayobyte: usable, with no dedicated SERP product. Let price and the countries you need decide.
Social media and multi-account management: Proxys.io. Proxys.io has the edge here. Why: fixed dedicated or mobile IPs per account. How Rayobyte compares: no SOCKS5 limits some account tools.
E-commerce price and stock monitoring: Rayobyte. Rayobyte has the edge here. Why: city targeting and low prices at volume. How Proxys.io compares: limited rotation for large catalog crawls.
Ad verification and geo-testing: Rayobyte. Rayobyte has the edge here. Why: fewer carrier or ASN controls. How Proxys.io compares: limited geo depth.

Tight budgets: close call. Both are reasonable choices here. Proxys.io: cheap per-IP rentals with unlimited bandwidth. Rayobyte: $2/GB from 50 GB and $0.90/GB at a terabyte. Let price and the countries you need decide.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. Proxys.io: 24-hour refund window instead of a trial. Rayobyte: Check current offer. Verification and payment rules differ too. Proxys.io: Light; crypto accepted. Rayobyte: Standard verification; US company. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test Proxys.io and Rayobyte before you commit
The quickest way to choose between Proxys.io and Rayobyte is a side-by-side test on the sites and countries you actually care about:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (Proxys.io: 24-hour refund window instead of a trial; Rayobyte: check current offer).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, Proxys.io comes out ahead in 1, Rayobyte in 3, and 2 are ties. That makes Rayobyte the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: Proxys.io is strongest for multi-account and affiliate work that needs fixed IPs, while Rayobyte is strongest for mid-to-high volume scraping on a budget. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
